title: 5 problems talent leaders are facing with AI in hiring, and what's working
summary: After talking with roughly 100 talent leaders, we found five problems keeping TA teams stuck: fraud, hiring redesign, disconnected tools, ROI, and security review. Here's what's working.
body_markdown:
Most talent leaders we know are working out how AI fits into hiring, ourselves included. Over the past year, our team at Zapier has worked alongside talent and people teams across industries. We've talked with roughly 100 leaders, at companies from high-growth startups to large enterprises.


Throughout our conversations, the same problems keep coming up. But so does a pattern in how the most forward-thinking TA teams handle them:


-


**They start with the technology they already own.** Talent teams are mapping their current tools and connecting them before adding to their tech stack.


-


**They let the people closest to the work build solutions.** Recruiters and coordinators are encouraged to build what they need so they can move quickly.


-


**They insist on guardrails.** AI fluency gets people building. Governance keeps what they build safe to scale. That means clear guardrails are set, and IT has oversight without being a bottleneck.


-


**They share AI skills and learnings.** Zapier's talent team, for example, takes useful AI skills that individuals have built and adapts them for the entire team, with a check for personal data at each step.


-


**They measure every build.** Each AI build has to improve candidate quality, team capacity, or the experience for candidates, hiring managers, and recruiters. The impact needs to be measurable.


Working with talent teams has allowed us to share best practices and brainstorm how to tackle some of the more pressing problems in TA today.

## 1. Fraud numbers keep climbing


**What we're seeing**


A year ago, it was startling when one company shared that 20% of its applicants were fraudulent. A few months later, 40% was a number we heard regularly. Now some leaders are seeing close to 80% on certain technical roles, and nobody expects it to level off.


Fraud has also gotten more sophisticated: we're seeing deepfaked interviews, proxy candidates, and coached answers. Leaders worry about wasted interview hours, and even more about letting a bad actor into the company.


**What's working**


The teams handling this best don't rely on one fraud check. They add checks at several points in the hiring process, and a candidate gets flagged only when several signals line up:


-


Application signals like IP and location mismatch, VPN and proxy use, and suspicious phone numbers


-


AI screening that checks the resume, the screen, and the interview against each other


-


Reference and background checks as the final gate


When several signals stack up, a recruiter takes a look. On our talent team, we built a system on tools we already had. Zaps monitor IP addresses and VPN use, and an[AI skill](https://zapier.com/blog/agent-skills/) flags inconsistencies for a recruiter to review. We also use fraud detection in all of our current tools, so we get signal and protection at every stage possible.


**Try this prompt:**


Prompt


```text
Use Zapier: Compare this candidate's resume, recruiter screen notes, and interview transcript. List any inconsistencies in dates, titles, employers, tools, or project details, and quote the lines that conflict. Don't decide whether it's fraud. Flag anything a recruiter should review.
```


## 2. Every team is redesigning hiring, and there's no shared playbook


**What we're seeing**


Candidates now use AI at every stage, so the old interview loop doesn't tell teams what it used to. Some leaders have rebuilt their interview and assessment process end to end because leadership mandated it. Others are still getting their own team comfortable with AI. Most are somewhere in between, and plenty say they aren't confident they're getting it right.


Wherever they are, the problem is the same: working out what an interview stage looks like once it's redesigned for candidates who use AI.


**What's working**


We've seen a few great approaches from teams further along:


-


A large tech company de-emphasized standard applications and created a "skip the line" path for candidates who showed proof of excellent work.


-


A workforce management company replaced "show me what you built" with live exercises that change as they go, testing iteration, judgment, and accountability.


-


An insurance company that couldn't find specialized sales talent started hiring for aptitude. It now runs 12-week internal academies for skills and AI fluency.


Start with the one stage your team trusts least. Define what a strong candidate looks like at that stage, then change how you assess it. Speed can come later.


Zapier can handle the work around the interview stage so recruiters can focus on creating the new assessment. For example, before the hiring manager intake, our recruiters run an AI skill that drafts the job description, interview structure, rubric, and interview questions into a hiring plan doc, so intake starts from a draft instead of a blank page. We also use Zapier to create a brief for every interviewer on what their stage is testing, and to prep the debrief.


That frees up time for us to create new assessments built around real work products or portfolios, live builds, and conversations.


**Try this prompt:**


Prompt


```text
Use Zapier: Pull the job description and the rubric for the [stage name] interview. Write a one-page brief for the interviewer: what this stage is testing, two or three questions that get at real work, and what strong, mixed, and weak answers sound like.
```


## 3. Teams have plenty of tools. They just aren't connected.


**What we're seeing**


The question we hear most is "which tool should we buy?" But that's not usually the right question. Often the team already has enough software, just no good way to connect it all.


-


One people team built personal AI agents, then sat in an IT queue waiting for approval to connect them to the ATS and HRIS.


-


A company that grew tenfold had its core operations automated, while everyone else ran one-off chatbots nobody could find or govern.


Tech stacks get more fragmented every year, which makes the connecting layer more valuable over time.


**What's working**


Zapier connects more than 10,000


apps, including Slack and the ATS, HRIS, and interview tools most talent teams already use.


Our talent team runs this way: applicant tracking, interview intelligence, AI interview screening, HRIS, headcount planning, Slack, and an AI assistant are all connected through Zapier. With[Zapier MCP](https://zapier.com/mcp) , recruiters can work across those apps from the AI agent they already use.


When a team starts by mapping what technology it already has, the conversation turns into an implementation plan quickly. And typically there's less of a need to purchase new tools. In fact, we've been able to eliminate some third-party tools by building more customized versions ourselves that run all on Zapier with automation and[AI steps](https://zapier.com/blog/ai-by-zapier-guide/) .


## 4. Hours saved no longer makes a strong ROI case


**What we're seeing**


The leaders furthest along in AI building have stopped leading ROI conversations with hours saved. Instead, most teams have landed on these three measures, with the understanding that every AI build should move at least one part.


**Measure**


**The question it answers**


Quality


Are we getting better candidates and better hires?


Efficiency


Can the team absorb more hiring without adding headcount?


Experience


Is the process better for candidates, hiring managers, and recruiters?


But quality of hire is a lagging measure. It shows up in ramp time, 30-, 90-, and 180-day performance, and the year-one review. Leaders want to connect interview decisions back to that data, and few have done it yet. We're working on this ourselves.


The business case that lands with executives is capacity: more hiring volume handled by the same team. But more and more teams are focusing on quality: how do we know that our AI implementation is leading to stronger candidates more likely to thrive?


**What's working**


Our talent team replaced a reference check tool that cost roughly $30K a year by building on Zapier. The new workflow pulls scorecards and interview transcripts, compares them against the rubric and job criteria, and writes candidate-specific reference questions aimed at real gaps.


That one build moved two parts of the ROI scorecard: more hiring capacity at lower cost, and reference checks that probe the gaps that matter for quality, surface better insights, and ultimately support better decision-making.


**Try this prompt:**


Prompt


```text
Use Zapier: Pull the job criteria, the interview rubric, and the interviewers' scorecards for this candidate. Find the two or three areas where the evidence is thinnest or interviewers disagreed. For each one, write a reference question that asks for a specific example, not a rating.
```


## 5. Security review sets the timeline


> Governance works like an electric fence. Once people know where the boundary is, they move freely. With no rules at all, the cautious ones freeze.


**What we're seeing**


People teams handle the most sensitive data in the company: things like compensation, performance, leave, immigration, investigations, and candidate information. Caution is the right default.


-


One team was still wary of connecting HR data to anything after a past data incident.


-


At another company, installing an approved AI assistant took about three weeks of security review.


**What's working**


Start with read-only access. That's what the team with the data incident did: they began with workflows that could read their HR data but not change it.


Zapier gives IT and legal the controls they ask about. Admins can restrict which actions each team runs inside an app, so a recruiting workflow can create candidate notes but never delete records, for example. Managed app connections keep credentials with the company, so workflows keep running when a recruiter leaves. Asset history shows what any workflow touched, and AI guardrails can flag personal data like Social Security numbers and bank account numbers before it reaches a model.


Whatever tools you use, hand IT and legal a one-page summary before they ask: what data the workflow touches, what it can and can't change, who owns the connection, and how you'd audit it.


## Questions to bring to your next leadership meeting


If any of these questions sound familiar, you're in good company. The teams making the most progress usually start with a better conversation at the leadership table.


Pick one question and bring it to your team this week. Use the answers to choose one stage or workflow to fix first, build it, and check it against the scorecard above.


**Theme**


**Ask your team**


AI adoption


Who's our most advanced AI user, and is what they do spreading beyond the enthusiasts?


Hiring redesign


Are we changing how we interview, or only how fast? Which stage do we trust least?


Connection


How many systems does a recruiter touch to move one candidate through one stage? What's still copied by hand?


Quality


How would we know we're getting better candidates as well as faster ones? If we freed 20% of the team's time next quarter, where would it go?


Fraud


When we catch a fraudulent candidate, how far into the process are we?


Readiness


If we wanted to roll something out next month, who has to say yes?
